The typescript itself, its photographs and its floor plans were not seen; the HABS bibliography lists 12 exterior views and small photographs of the basement and two principal floor plans in it (data p. 6).
glessner_story_of_a_house_1923.note: The owner describing his own house thirty-six years after he moved in, and seventeen years after the scene year. It is dated testimony and is read that way: what it says of the building's CONSTRUCTION ('the roofs are of red baked tiles, unglazed, the outside walls on the streets are of Wellesley granite') describes the house as built and so carries to 1904, while what it says of the house's CURRENT state carries only to 1923 ('the carriage house and stables (now garage)' dates a conversion to before March 1923 and says nothing about 1904). It also records that 'by special arrangement the same brick were used in the adjoining house, so that all walls of the courtyard are of the same texture and color' - the courtyard's south side is the neighbouring house's wall - and that the house was criticised for 'the narrow windows in its north side along 18th Street, just enough to light the narrow corridors'.
what_it_supplies: the roof covering as built: red baked tiles, unglazed
the street walls of Wellesley granite; all walls lined with hollow brick
the courtyard elevation of common brick of slightly pinkish colour with grey limestone trimmings, matched in the adjoining house's wall
the courtyard entrance from the alley, used on moving day in December 1887
Virginia creeper on the courtyard walls (carried from the old house, 1887) and Boston ivy on the street front (from plants sent after June 1887)
the service entrance 'through the great arch on Eighteenth Street'; the Eighteenth Street door and back stairs
outside iron-work Bower-Barffed rather than painted
what_it_does_not_supply: any dimension
the extent of the ivy or creeper in any year
when the stable became a garage
glessner_story_of_a_house_1923.url_basis: Link is to HABS ILL-1015, whose data pages transcribe the1923 text. The underlying original typescript was not consulted; text-only/check-required rights remain unchanged.

habs_glessner_house_il_1015_data_pages.note: Two documents in one, and they are cited separately. The HABS architectural description (1963) is this record. Pages 7-21 also transcribe John J. Glessner's March 1923 booklet The Story of a House, which is period testimony by the owner and is cited as glessner_story_of_a_house_1923 so that its date is carried with it. THE ALTERATIONS PARAGRAPH IS WHAT MAKES THE DRAWINGS USABLE FOR 1904: it lists what the September 1946 research-centre conversion changed (stable loft and basement partitioned, stable door replaced, loft door closed up, stable/kitchen/laundry fixtures and the coal furnace removed, school-room woodwork painted, the door of the underpass on the east facade replaced, the courtyard entirely paved as a parking lot) and says the original plan, finishes and permanent furniture were left untouched. It names no change to the masonry envelope or the roofs. The legal description on p. 1: Block 9, lots 38, 39 and 40 of the Assessor's Division of the SW fractional 1/4 of Section 22, T39N, R14E; Glessner bought lots 39, 40 and the north 17 feet of lot 38 on March 24, 1885 (Book 502A pp. 77-79; Document 616860). Note the wall-material name: 'Wellesley Granite' (p. 21), which is also Glessner's 1923 word; the house museum's own page says Braggville pink granite (recorded in the Prairie library's dossier as G02). The disagreement is carried, not resolved.
what_it_supplies: the exterior construction as surveyed in 1963: foundations of Joliet limestone ending at the ground line; brick walls faced with alternately six- and eight-inch sheets of granite with deeper returns at openings; courtyard walls of light pink brick with Joliet limestone lintels and sills; steeply pitched gabled roofs covered with tar-covered terracotta tiles six inches wide, five inches exposed; copper sheathing on the roof of the entrance-hall bow
the original east carriage (porte-cochere) door as seen in a 1945 photograph: two heavily panelled leaves with heavy iron straps and latches
the list of 1946 alterations, which is the phase filter every 1963 dimension has to pass for 1904
the legal description and the March 1885 purchase of lots 39, 40 and the north 17 ft of lot 38
what_it_does_not_supply: the widths of lots 38-40 in feet: the lot sizes of the Assessor's Division block are not stated
the date the stable became a garage, the date the roof tiles were tarred, or any other change between 1887 and 1946 that it does not list
measurements: the data pages describe; the drawings (habs_glessner_house_il_1015_drawings) measure

Sheet 6 heights are referred to a local datum, '0.00 AT DOOR' (the Prairie Avenue front door sill), with the sidewalk before the doorway at -0.74; they are not Chicago City Datum. Section A-A (sheet 4) has no printed heights: its heights are measured off the drawing and referred to the grade it draws at the 18th Street wall.

chicago_revised_municipal_code_1905.citation: The Revised Municipal Code of Chicago of 1905. Passed March 20, 1905. Revised and codified by Edgar Bronson Tolman, Corporation Counsel, assisted by William H. Arthur and Roswell B. Mason. Chicago: published by authority of the City Council (book form October 15, 1905); Rochester, N.Y.: The Lawyers' Co-operative Publishing Company, 1905.
chicago_revised_municipal_code_1905.author: City of Chicago (E. B. Tolman, codifier)
chicago_revised_municipal_code_1905.describes_date: the general ordinances in force on 20 March 1905
chicago_revised_municipal_code_1905.repository: Internet Archive, digitized by Google from a library copy (Chicago School of Civics and Philanthropy stamp on the title page)
chicago_revised_municipal_code_1905.locator: Chapter LIX, Sidewalks, Article I, Construction of Sidewalks: sec. 2062 (Portland cement concrete walks; printed pp. 548-549), the 'Slope' and 'Curbage' sections of the concrete specification (p. 552; the OCR numbers both 2066), sec. 2068 (stone sidewalks; pp. 552-553), sec. 2072 (sidewalk widths -- curbs; pp. 554-555), sec. 2077 (fixed width -- grass plats; p. 555). Read again for T-1728 (materials): sec. 1944 (the kinds of 'artificial pavement of a permanent character': granite, asphalt, macadam, brick, cedar block, creosoted block; p. 517), sec. 2061 (the sidewalk specifications bind every walk not laid under a special-assessment ordinance; p. 548), sec. 2066 'Curbage' (concrete curbage with concrete walks; p. 552), sec. 2068 (stone sidewalks of limestone; pp. 552-553), sec. 2070 (cinder walks between wooden curbs of split cedar posts faced with hemlock plank; pp. 553-554), secs. 2078-2079 (a wooden sidewalk may be repaired but none may be built; p. 556).
chicago_revised_municipal_code_1905.rights_note: A 1905 publication of the City of Chicago; public domain in the United States.
chicago_revised_municipal_code_1905.access_notes: Read 2026-09-28 (T-0474) in the Internet Archive's OCR text of the Google scan (the djvu.txt at archived_url, 2,943,992 bytes); the passages below were read in that text at the printed page numbers it carries, and quoted as the OCR gives them with the scanning errors corrected. The page images were not opened. Re-read 2026-09-29 (T-1728) in the same OCR text for the materials sections added to the locator.
chicago_revised_municipal_code_1905.note: A codification, not a new enactment: its title page says it contains 'all the general ordinances of the city in force March 20, A.D. 1905', eight and a half months after the 1904 scene date. It is used for three street-section figures, each carried to 1 July 1904 as INFERRED, not attested, because the code does not date its individual sections: sec. 2072 -- 'All sidewalks which may hereafter be ordered by the city council ... shall be of the width herein specified, unless a different width shall be specified in the order, to wit: ... on streets sixty-six feet and under eighty feet in width, fourteen feet; ... on streets fifty feet and under sixty feet in width, ten feet ... When built of full width, a substantial curbing of stone or white-oak plank, not less than three inches in thickness well tied in, shall be laid on the outer edge of the sidewalk'; sec. 2062 -- 'All walks to be laid on a line one foot from and parallel with the lot line unless otherwise ordered by special ordinance', and 'All work on 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24 and 25 foot walks to be laid out in blocks five feet by six feet in size'; sec. 2077 -- 'on all streets where courts or open spaces are allowed for planting trees or for grass plats, the same shall not be covered with plank or other material'. The 'Slope' sections of the concrete and stone specifications (pp. 552, 553) give the grade across the sidewalk space: 'a uniform incline from the street line toward the curb line, with a fall of one inch in every three feet'.
what_it_supplies: The city's default width of the sidewalk space (street line to curb line) on a street of a given width: 14 ft on streets 66 to 80 ft wide, 10 ft on streets 50 to 60 ft wide (sec. 2072)
Where a walk stands inside that space: one foot from and parallel with the lot line, unless a special ordinance says otherwise (sec. 2062)
The walk widths the city's paving specification anticipates (5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24 and 25 ft; sec. 2062), which bound a reconstructed walk width
That the rest of the sidewalk space could be a planted court or grass plat (sec. 2077), i.e. a parkway
The curb's minimum thickness where one was required (3 in, stone or white oak; sec. 2072) and the cross-fall of the sidewalk space (1 in in 3 ft toward the curb; the 'Slope' sections, pp. 552-553)

The period's permitted MATERIALS, as bounds (T-1728): walks of Portland cement concrete in 5 x 6 ft blocks, of limestone, or of cinders between wooden curbs, and no new wooden walk (secs. 2062, 2068, 2070, 2079); curbing of stone or white-oak plank (sec. 2072) or concrete with a concrete walk (sec. 2066); roadways of granite, asphalt, macadam, brick, cedar block or creosoted block (sec. 1944)
what_it_does_not_supply: The sidewalk actually laid on any particular block, or its date: every width in sec. 2072 yields to 'a different width ... specified in the order', and a block-level special-assessment ordinance or photograph is what would say what Prairie Avenue had
The width of a walk within the sidewalk space: the code lists permitted walk widths and chooses none
Any material for a particular block (T-1728 owns the surfaces)
The curb's reveal (its height above the gutter) or the roadway's crown
Whether the sections were in force in exactly this form on 1 July 1904; the code is dated 20 March 1905
